newsitem.title: SPAIN: BOS intervention seen stifling peseta strength.
newsitem.headline: BOS intervention seen stifling peseta strength.

text.p: Expectations that Spain will enter a European single currency are likely to exert upward influence on the peseta until the end of 1996, but Bank of Spain intervention will dilute any such pressures, analysts said.

Traders said on Thursday they did not expect any significant deviation in peseta/mark from an 84.10 to 84.30 band in the next month and any short-term bumps would be dictated by trends in other cross rates.

"The peseta will continue to be stable in a narrow range because of the influence of the Bank of Spain. The central bank likes a very rangebound peseta because stability is one of the key factors for European Monetary Union," said Juan Antonio Mielgo, economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
Traders said they suspected the Bank of Spain had continued to intervene in the market in recent weeks, buying marks to maintain a peseta/mark level just above 84.00.

Many analysts said that in the absence of any concrete comments from the Bundesbank on whether it believed Spain would enter EMU, optimistic expectations would gather speed. But they added the market would keep a watchful eye on a number of key factors up to the year-end.

The passage of Spain's 1997 budget which aims to reduce the deficit to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in line with Maastricht criteria, had already been discounted by the market, analysts said.
"More important will be the assessment that the European Commission makes of the 1997 budget in its autumn forecasts in November," said Jose Luis Alzola, economist at Salomon Brothers.
"This will reveal whether the Commission believes a three percent target for next year is feasible," he added.

Other factors which analysts said could affect the peseta included October figures for the state deficit which will shed some light on whether Spain is likely to meet this year's budget deficit target of 4.4 percent of GDP.

Spain is currently in negotiations with the European Commission after failing to meet its 1995 budget target, which could put at risk convergence funds totalling almost 0.3 percent GDP, an analyst said.
But analysts said although the European Commission would not want to lose face over the problem, it was unlikely the funds would not be awarded.
Signs of inflationary pressures will also be rigidly assessed as a key factor for entry into EMU and for the possibility of further interest rate cuts, analysts said.
"I think we'll have inflation below three percent at the beginning of 1997 and trade unions accepting moderate wage demands that will make the inflation target more credible," said Alzola.

Most analysts said they expected a cut before the end of the year or at the beginning of next year. But the Bank of Spain would want to make sure that inflation had dropped to below three percent and that the drop was sustainable, they added.

"If inflation rebounds, that would change market expectations from an interest rate cut to a hike. In these circumstances the peseta would come under considerable pressure as Spain would be further from meeting the Maastrict criteria," a trader said.

Spain plans to bring inflation down to 3.5 percent in 1996 and 2.6 percent in 1997 to meet the Maastricht convergence criteria for EMU. The consumer price index rose 3.7 percent year-on-year in August.
